explanation: A lane is a longitudinal strip of the carriageway wide enough for a single line of moving vehicles; the correct number in the picture points to that marked traffic strip, not the shoulder or divider shown elsewhere in the illustration.
A center reservation (divider) is the raised or marked area separating the two opposing traffic flows on a wide road, and is distinct in the picture from an ordinary lane or the hard shoulder.

The hard shoulder is the paved strip beyond the outer traffic lane, reserved for emergencies and breakdowns rather than for normal through-driving, which is why it is marked separately in the illustration.

Traffic law exempts only authorized security and emergency vehicles from the one-way rule, since they alone may need to travel against the flow to respond to urgent situations; every other vehicle must follow the signed direction.

The law allows a driver to leave their lane at any time, provided the maneuver creates no danger or disturbance to any other road user, since the general duty of care governs lane changes rather than a fixed prohibition or technique.

A vehicle may deviate from its line of driving whenever doing so causes no risk or disturbance to any other passerby, reflecting the general duty-of-care principle rather than a blanket ban or a rule tied to speed or sharpness of the turn.

A right turn must be made from the right-hand lane into the right-hand lane of the road being entered, at a reasonable speed and without creating danger or disturbance, rather than in a wide arc or from any arbitrary lane.

At a junction with marked turning lanes, a right turn must be made only from the lane the signs and markings designate for that movement, feeding into the corresponding lane of the road being entered, not from any other lane.

Before turning right, a driver must confirm no vehicle, such as a cyclist or motorcyclist, is coming up on their right side, since such a vehicle could be struck if the driver turns across its path without checking.

The turn must be executed only from the lane whose markings and arrows are designated for that direction, leading into the matching lane of the road being entered, following the signposted lane discipline shown at the junction.

Lane markings and signage at this junction assign a specific lane for the turn into the matching lane of the entered road; turning from an unmarked lane or into the wrong lane would violate the signposted lane assignment.

The signed lane markings at this junction assign a particular lane for the turn into street C, feeding into a matching lane of that road, so the driver must follow the exact lane-to-lane path shown by the signs.
According to the junction's lane markings, the turn is only correct when made between the specific lanes the signposted arrows connect for this movement, not any other lane combination.

The posted lane arrows at this junction dedicate a specific lane to this turn and connect it to a matching lane of the entered road, so the driver must follow that path rather than any other lane combination.

Turning from street A to street B, the signed lane markings direct traffic from one specific lane into a matching lane of the entered road, and the driver must follow the lane the signs assign for that particular turn.

Turning from street C to street A, the junction's signage assigns a specific lane for this movement, feeding into a matching lane of the entered road, as shown by the marked lane arrows in the diagram.

A U-turn is legal anywhere it causes no danger or disturbance to other road users, as long as no road sign specifically prohibits it there; it is not restricted to intersections or to roads with a minimum number of lanes.

A U-turn is forbidden wherever a driver approaching from another direction would not be able to see the turning vehicle in time, since such a blind maneuver risks a collision the other driver cannot anticipate or avoid.

A left U-turn may be made from the left-hand lane or from any other lane, as long as no road marking or sign specifically bars a turn from that lane, rather than being restricted only to the leftmost or a straight-arrow lane.

Reversing is legal only when it is actually necessary and can be carried out without endangering, obstructing, or disturbing any other road user, so it is neither an absolute prohibition nor unconditionally free.

When two vehicles meet on a narrow, flat road, both drivers should slow down and move toward the edge of the roadway to leave room for each other, since safety here depends on mutual accommodation rather than vehicle size or local custom.

On a narrow, steep incline the descending vehicle must give way and stop if required, because a vehicle going uphill loses more of its hard-won momentum and traction if it is forced to stop and restart on the slope.

Since traffic keeps to the right, overtaking must be done from the left side of the vehicle ahead, moving into the lane used by oncoming or faster traffic; passing on the right is not a general legal option.

Passing on the right is allowed once the vehicle ahead has indicated and positioned itself to turn left, because it is effectively vacating the through lane and will not be in the overtaking vehicle's path.

You may legally pass another vehicle on its right side when you are driving within a lane designated for that purpose, such as a bus lane you are entitled to use, rather than cutting across the road's edge or shoulder.

A vehicle sitting in a left-turn-only lane is about to leave the through lane, so passing it on its right side is permitted since the overtaking driver remains in their own proper lane while the other vehicle turns away.

The points system operates alongside any court-imposed penalty as a separate administrative track for monitoring repeat offenders, so a driver can be fined or sentenced and still accumulate points for the same offense.

When a driver is legitimately traveling in a lane designated only for a right turn, using that lane to pass a vehicle in the adjacent through lane is not an unlawful right-side overtake, since they remain in their own lane's path.

Overtaking is permitted only when the road ahead is clear enough to complete the maneuver and return to the lane without endangering or disturbing any other road user, not only when the vehicle ahead is slow or a motorcycle.

Overtaking is banned whenever visibility is poor or the field of view is obstructed, because the driver cannot then be sure the opposing lane is clear far enough ahead to complete the maneuver safely.

Overtaking is completely forbidden within 100 meters of a railway crossing regardless of the vehicle type being passed or whether a train is currently visible, since the added risk near a crossing makes any attempt too dangerous.

Drivers must not overtake, or even attempt to overtake, as they approach a pedestrian crossing, because doing so could hide a crossing pedestrian from view or force a vehicle onto the crossing at an unsafe moment.

Overtaking is prohibited within an intersection's boundaries because of the added risk from crossing traffic, with a narrow exception for passing a two-wheeled vehicle, which poses far less risk of a serious collision.

A driver may not overtake a vehicle that has stopped before an intersection, a pedestrian crossing, or a railway crossing, since that vehicle may be yielding to a hazard, such as cross traffic or a train, that is not yet visible to the overtaking driver.

The vehicle being overtaken should move as far toward the edge of the road as it safely can while keeping its speed steady, making room for the overtaking vehicle without creating unpredictable braking or acceleration.
A driver forced to travel slowly because of a heavy load or a steep gradient must use the paved hard shoulder where one is available, so as not to obstruct normal-speed traffic in the regular lanes.

Traffic law requires keeping whatever gap from the vehicle ahead is needed to stop in time and avoid a collision under the current speed and road conditions, rather than relying on a single fixed distance that fits every situation.

The legal floor for the following gap is the distance covered in one second of travel, since anything closer leaves no real separation, even though safer practice, based on reaction-time studies, recommends a larger two-to-three second gap.

Reasonable speed is defined by law as a speed that lets the driver keep full control of the vehicle given the actual road, traffic, and weather conditions and any posted signs, not a fixed number or the vehicle's mechanical top speed.

A driver must slow down whenever continuing at the current speed would put their own vehicle, another road user, or property at risk, since this general duty of care overrides any specific posted speed limit.

The law requires slowing down whenever the road is obstructed, visibility is poor, or the road has sharp bends, since these conditions reduce a driver's ability to see hazards and to stop or steer away from them in time.

The scenario shown calls for reducing speed rather than a full stop, a honk, or acceleration, because the depicted hazard or caution point requires the driver to retain full control while approaching it, not necessarily to halt outright.
Drivers must slow down around an animal on or near the road, since a sudden loud engine or a close pass can startle the animal into an unpredictable movement directly into the vehicle's path.
The picture indicates a hazard or caution situation calling for reduced speed so the driver retains full control and reaction time, rather than stopping outright, honking, or accelerating.

An emergency stop is justified only as a last resort to prevent a road accident that cannot be avoided in any other way, since braking hard without real cause creates its own collision risk for following traffic.

Emergency braking for a reason other than avoiding an accident is allowed only for testing the brakes, and only when it causes no danger or disturbance to any other road user, making it a narrow, conditional exception.

Only a motor vehicle that is both permitted and mechanically capable of maintaining the speed shown on the freeway's sign may enter, since a slower vehicle would create a serious hazard mixing with the freeway's high-speed traffic.
An all-terrain vehicle's maximum permitted speed is capped at 40 km/h on every type of road, including freeways, reflecting this vehicle category's lower design speed and stability limits.

The legally required interval for a vehicle roadworthiness test varies by vehicle type and age, as set by law, rather than following a single uniform two-year rule that applies to every vehicle without distinction.
For a private passenger car, the default maximum speed on a freeway, unless a sign states otherwise, is 110 km/h, as set out in the maximum permitted speed regulations for this road category.

An inter-urban road with a constructed central median divider carries a default maximum speed of 90 km/h for a private passenger vehicle, higher than an undivided inter-urban road because the physical divider removes the risk of head-on conflict.

Unless signs state otherwise, a private passenger vehicle's default maximum speed is 50 km/h in an urban area and 80 km/h on an ordinary inter-urban road, reflecting the higher pedestrian and junction density found in town.

A regulatory speed sign of this type sets a maximum, meaning the vehicle's driving speed must not exceed the number shown; it establishes an upper limit rather than a minimum, and applies generally rather than to a single vehicle category.

A 'play street,' where children and pedestrians are expected to be present, carries a legal maximum speed of 30 km/h, lower than an ordinary residential street, so that any unavoidable close encounter remains survivable.

Approaching a railway crossing, a driver must reduce speed enough that the vehicle can be stopped before the tracks if that turns out to be necessary, rather than driving through at normal speed or requiring a full stop in every case.

A driver must always slow down when approaching a railway barrier controlled by a traffic light, regardless of whether a train is currently visible or audible, since the crossing remains a heightened-risk area at all times.

The law sets a specific fallback order for where to stop at a railway crossing: at the stop line if marked, otherwise before the barrier, and if there is no barrier, at least four meters before the nearest rail, keeping the vehicle clear of danger in every configuration.

Once a train is seen, heard, or signaled by a warning device, the driver must stop before the crossing and wait until it has fully passed; attempting to cross ahead of the train, at any speed, is never permitted.

When a stop sign is posted before a railway crossing, the driver must make a full, deliberate stop, turn off any radio or media playing, and open the window to listen for an approaching train, not just perform the usual brief stop-and-go.

Driving through a railway crossing is prohibited for as long as the barrier is moving in either direction or lying horizontal, since a moving or lowered barrier signals that a train is approaching or still clearing the crossing.

The duty to stop before a railway crossing is triggered by an approaching train actually being seen, heard, or announced by a warning signal, not solely by the presence of a particular static sign at that location.

If a warning signal activates before a driver reaches the crossing, they must stop and not proceed, since the signal itself creates the stopping obligation regardless of whether an oncoming train can personally be seen.

Direction indicators must be used whenever a driver is about to pull away, turn, or move out of their lane, since this signaling duty is general and continuous, not limited to specific locations such as crossings or particular turn types.
Signaling is mandatory before beginning any deviation from the driving lane and must continue until the maneuver is complete, regardless of how small or seemingly insignificant the lane shift is.

The rule requires giving the turn signal at whatever time and place will let other road users actually notice and react to it, rather than following a fixed distance figure that might not fit every situation.
A braking signal is given automatically through the vehicle's brake lights when the pedal is pressed, and is not something communicated through hand signals or the direction indicators.

If the vehicle's electric turn signals stop working, the driver is required to give hand signals instead, regardless of weather conditions or time of day, so other road users still receive adequate warning of the intended maneuver.

When the electric signaling system malfunctions, the law requires the driver to signal with an outstretched left hand as a substitute, rather than skipping signals or continuing to drive without them until reaching a garage.

Seeing a direction indicator on the vehicle ahead, a following driver should slow down, and stop if necessary, to let that vehicle safely complete the turn or lane change it has signaled for, rather than pressing on regardless.

When using the horn to signal, the sound should last no longer than needed to achieve its warning purpose, since prolonged or repeated honking causes unnecessary disturbance without adding any safety value.

In an urban area the horn may be used only to prevent an imminent danger that cannot be avoided any other way; it is not for general or continuous use, and using it routinely in town is not permitted.

In this illustration a 'road' refers to the entire right-of-way used by traffic between two points, including its lanes, shoulders, and dividers together, rather than any single lane or divider marked separately within it.

When crossing a sidewalk while exiting a driveway or private property, the driver must slow down, and stop if necessary, to let pedestrians using the sidewalk pass safely, since they have priority over a vehicle emerging from a non-road exit.

Once past the sidewalk and about to enter or cross the road itself from a private exit, the driver must give way to vehicles already approaching on that road, since a vehicle emerging from a driveway never has right of way over through traffic.

At an intersection with no priority signs, a driver turning left must give way to vehicles coming straight through from the opposite direction and to vehicles approaching from the right, since a left turn crosses both of their paths.

A one-way road is identified in the illustration by its directional arrows or signage that permits travel in a single direction only, distinguishing it from the two-way streets shown elsewhere in the picture.

Leaving a private yard, a petrol station, or a property entrance, the driver must slow down and stop if needed to let pedestrians cross safely, applying the same sidewalk-priority rule as any other driveway exit.

Exiting premises, a gas station, or a house's access road, the driver must give way both to vehicles already on the road being entered and to any pedestrians on the pavement being crossed, since the duty covers both groups, not just one.

Approaching this intersection, the driver must slow down, and stop if required, to give way as the situation demands, rather than assuming the right of way or accelerating through regardless of other traffic.
This sign instructs the driver to give right of way specifically to traffic on the roadway to their left, marking that direction as having priority at this particular junction configuration.

A stop sign requires the driver to stop and then give way to every other vehicle entering or approaching the intersection from any other roadway, not merely to traffic from one particular direction or only when a police officer directs it.

When a stop sign and stop line are present, the driver must stop right before and close to that line, since the line marks the exact legal stopping point rather than leaving the driver free to stop anywhere short of the junction.

Without a marked stop line, the correct stopping point is wherever the driver gains a clear view of the traffic crossing their path, since the purpose of stopping is to actually be able to check for oncoming vehicles before proceeding.

This sign requires a full stop followed by giving way to other traffic, unlike a simple yield sign that only requires giving way without necessarily requiring the vehicle to come to a complete stop first.

In this situation the driver must stop before the junction and not enter it at all, since proceeding into the intersection, even partway, would leave the vehicle blocking crossing traffic or trapped without a clear path through.

A flashing yellow traffic light is a caution signal, not a fixed right-of-way rule for one direction, so drivers must slow down, and stop if the actual traffic situation demands it, using judgment rather than assuming priority.

Crossing railway tracks is permitted only once the crossing is entirely clear, the barrier is fully raised, and it can be crossed safely; a barrier that has merely started to lift does not yet make the crossing safe.

Before pulling away from a stop or parking spot, the driver must signal appropriately and actually confirm that merging into traffic will not endanger anyone, rather than assuming the signal alone entitles them to right of way.

Approaching a pedestrian crossing that people are actively using, a driver must always slow down, and stop if necessary, to let them finish crossing safely, regardless of which direction the pedestrians happen to be moving.

A pedestrian crossing split by a traffic island is treated legally as two separate crossings, so a driver must independently give way to pedestrians on each half rather than treating the whole thing as one continuous crossing.

When a driving lane is obstructed, the driver must follow the instructions of a police officer, a signaler, or the relevant road sign for how to proceed around it, rather than deciding alone which side to pass or assuming automatic right of way.

If a driving lane is blocked by an obstruction, the driver must give way to vehicles coming from the opposite direction while maneuvering around it, since the obstructed side is the one that must yield to unobstructed traffic.

In an urban area, stopping, standing, or parking is permitted wherever it is not specifically prohibited by law or a road sign and does not disturb traffic, making it a conditional permission rather than an unconditional right or a blanket ban.

Descending a long, steep hill, the driver should slow down and shift into a lower gear appropriate to the grade so the engine helps control speed, rather than coasting in neutral or relying solely on continuous braking, which can overheat the brakes.

Stopping on the hard shoulder of a designated main inter-urban road is reserved for vehicles like public-works or IDF vehicles actually carrying out their official duties, not for general commercial or private use.

Loading or unloading passengers on a freeway is completely prohibited under all circumstances, since pedestrians stepping out into high-speed motorway traffic create an extreme and unnecessary danger.

Stopping, standing, or parking on a freeway is banned by default, with the only exception being where a specific sign expressly permits it; a wide road edge alone does not create an exception to this rule.
A vehicle forced to stand in the road must be marked with a warning triangle placed behind it, visible from at least 100 meters, giving approaching drivers enough distance and time to react safely.

Stopping or parking is prohibited wherever the vehicle obstructs traffic flow or blocks a road sign from being seen, since either effect creates a hazard for other road users regardless of curb markings or whether the vehicle is locked.

Parking on the left side of a two-way street is forbidden because vehicles should stand on the right in the direction of travel, and a vehicle parked facing or beside opposing traffic creates a hazard regardless of the street's width or number of lanes.
